Background
A refinery turnaround is a scheduled multi-week shutdown of major processing units (such as crude distillation units, fluid catalytic crackers, cokers, or hydrotreaters) for legally mandated inspections, catalyst replacement, and heavy repairs. Because major turnarounds require months of parts procurement and specialized contractor crews, operators adjust timing based on both mechanical inspection limits and refining margins. A crack spread measures the gross margin between crude oil input and refined fuel output (42 gallons per barrel of product minus crude cost), before operating, energy, compliance, and turnaround expenses.

America's Refiners Drowned Their Own Gasoline Windfall

U.S. refiners spent 2026 squeezing less gasoline out of every barrel to chase diesel and jet fuel margins, and they still produced enough gasoline to nearly wipe out their margins on it. Gasoline yields averaged below 45% in the first eight months of the year and fell below the previous five-year low in every month, according to Energy Information Administration (EIA) data. Jet fuel's share of output topped 12% in March for the first time on record and stayed at or above that level through August.
U.S. refiners also raised crude processing by 500,000 barrels per day in Q2 and by another 500,000 bpd in Q3. The gasoline crack spread, adjusted for real-world crude prices and renewable fuel credits, is now "barely positive" and has turned negative in some parts of the country, Will Kubzansky wrote in Bloomberg's Energy Daily newsletter on Monday. U.S. diesel margins stood above $80 a barrel on Friday, their lowest level since mid-July. Kubzansky put the turn down to the refiners' own supply response after a year of operating close to maximum capacity. The Middle East hasn’t changed. Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz have intensified in recent weeks, and disruption to fuel shipments from the Persian Gulf is in its ninth month.
In the week to November 13, U.S. refinery utilization rose to 95.7%, and gasoline inventories climbed by 5.2 million barrels to 215.9 million barrels, according to the EIA's weekly report. That build was more than three times the 1.6 million barrels analysts polled by Reuters had expected. Distillate stocks rose by 1.6 million barrels to 104.9 million.
The two fuels are now on opposite ends of the five-year range. Reuters columnist Ron Bousso wrote on Monday that U.S. gasoline stocks are above their five-year average, while distillate inventories are about 15% below it. U.S. diesel margins have fallen from a record $118 a barrel in mid-September to about $80, and the U.S. crack spread has dropped from a record $72 a barrel to about $41.
Drivers are seeing the decline at the pump.

...

Third-quarter results show how far diesel out-earned gasoline before the slide. Valero Energy reported net income of $6.8 billion, against $1.1 billion a year earlier, and a refining margin of $39.24 per barrel of throughput, against $13.14, according to its third-quarter release. On the U.S. Gulf Coast, Valero's margin on ultra-low-sulfur diesel averaged $72.27 a barrel over Brent in the quarter, up from $21.05 a year earlier and three times its gasoline margin of $24.08. Marathon Petroleum ran its refineries at 100% of crude capacity and lifted its refining and marketing margin to $45.70 a barrel from $17.60. Shares of both companies have doubled this year, according to the Motley Fool.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its November Oil Market Report that refining margins weakened almost everywhere in October, and that lower gasoline prices weighed on U.S. refiners' profits even as they benefited from cheaper crude. The agency expects global refinery runs to rise from a seasonal low of 81.3 million bpd in October to 84.7 million bpd in December.
Kubzansky wrote that crack spreads could widen again, and named Russia as one catalyst. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on October 30 that Ukrainian drone attacks "could certainly lead to a decrease in export volumes" of diesel, according to TASS. On November 18, Reuters reported, citing sources, that drone attacks had nearly halved Russia's oil refining in November.

Oil's Iran war recovery masks a stubborn diesel shortage

11/23/2026 8:00:00 AM
    
Nine months into the biggest energy shock in modern history, the oil market's recovery is surprisingly swift, but plentiful crude supplies are masking a stubborn diesel shortage that could yet upend fuel markets.
Benchmark Brent crude LCOc1 has dropped by more than 20% since the start of the month to just over $90 a barrel. Recovering Middle East exports and fading fears of a major escalation in the US-Iran war have driven the decline. The retreat comes after high fuel prices pummeled US President Donald Trump's Republican Party in this month's midterm elections.
Crucially, gasoline and diesel prices have also retreated from their peaks, offering consumers some relief and promising to ease inflationary pressures on governments.
In Europe, a major diesel importer, futures prices LGOc1 have fallen by a quarter from their September peak to around $160 a barrel, but they remain nearly twice their level at the start of the year.
In the US, the world's largest refiner and oil consumer, retail diesel prices have slipped below $6 a gallon to a two-month low, while gasoline was down below $4 for the first time since August, according to GasBuddy.
Any lasting recovery hinges on easing Middle East tensions, however, and that is far from assured. Iran has stepped up attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz and struck facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait, while Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi militia continues to target Saudi Arabia.

...

Commercial US crude stockpiles have risen by around 2% since the start of November after hitting their lowest point since 2018 in September, according to US Energy Information Administration data. China also appeared to add to its vast crude inventories in October.
Crude, in other words, is no longer the market's biggest headache.
Diesel divide. Fuel markets remain considerably tighter. The tightness, though, is tilted heavily toward diesel following the loss of refining capacity in the Middle East and months of Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
In 2025, the Middle East and Russia together accounted for more than 2 million bpd, or nearly 30%, of the 7.4 million bpd of diesel shipped by sea. Global seaborne diesel exports have averaged just 6.2 million bpd so far this year despite sharply higher US shipments, explaining why diesel remains scarce.
US inventories have recovered slightly in recent weeks, largely because US exports have fallen due to soaring tanker rates. Distillate inventories, which include diesel and heating oil, have rebounded by almost 6% since the end of October, when they fell below 100 million barrels for the first time since 2003. They remain around 15% below their five-year average, however, leaving little cushion as the northern hemisphere enters the winter heating season.
Gasoline tells a very different story.
The market has been far less exposed to the loss of Middle Eastern and Russian supplies, allowing inventories to recover much faster. US gasoline stocks have risen by nearly 6% since hitting their lowest level since 2014 in late September and are now back above their five-year average.
That growing divergence between diesel scarcity and gasoline abundance is becoming the defining feature of the refining market, which continues to operate at very high rates.
Mixed feelings. The split is even more obvious in refining margins.
US gasoline margins of around $20 a barrel are back below their pre-war levels. While diesel margins have retreated from an all-time high of $118 a barrel in mid-September to around $80, they are still twice their pre-war level. European diesel refining margins have similarly retreated from around $90 a barrel in September to $60, but they remain roughly triple their 2025 average.
Falling product prices have also sharply reduced US refining profitability. The benchmark US refining crack spread CL321-1=R has dropped from a record-high $72 a barrel in September to around $41 now. That is the lowest since April, but it is still exceptionally strong by historical standards.

* Oil prices have plunged more than 20% in November, with Brent falling below $90 as recovering Gulf crude exports push global markets toward oversupply.
* Diesel supplies remain critically tight, with disruptions in the Middle East and Russia removing roughly 2 million bpd of exports and keeping refining margins elevated.
* Diesel prices and margins are easing but remain well above pre-war levels, with low inventories and potential winter demand threatening to prolong shortages into 2027.
Oil prices have tumbled by more than 20% so far in November with Brent Crude sinking below $90 per barrel this week, as market participants and analysts bet on continued recovery of crude oil flows from the Strait of Hormuz.
The oil market balance appears to be tipping into oversupply, forecasters say, and crude prices are reflecting this notion.
But the product markets, especially the diesel market, remain tight, despite recent declines in diesel margins and retail prices.
Retail diesel prices in the United States last week fell below $6 per gallon for the first time in over two months, and gasoline prices have also dropped below $4 a gallon in recent weeks amid the slide in crude oil prices.
Diesel refining margins, however, remain double or triple compared to before the Iran war, depending on the region, even if they had dropped off from the all-time highs hit in September.

Crude vs Diesel Markets

The expected glut in the crude oil market is not directly translating into an abundance of diesel supplies. Shipments of diesel from the Middle East remain a fraction compared to before the war, while Russia’s diesel exports have collapsed as Ukraine is regularly taking Russian refineries offline in a massive campaign to cut fuel supply to the front line and export revenues for the Kremlin.
Despite their best efforts so far this year, refineries elsewhere cannot fully offset the estimated loss of about 2 million barrels per day (bpd) of total diesel exports from the Middle East and Russia combined.
Diesel margins, futures, and retail prices have eased this month, and inventories in the U.S. have started to gradually increase, but the market will take months to rebalance, assuming there is no escalation in the Middle East.
“The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran,” the International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its Oil Market Report for November.
Observed oil inventories rose by 52 million barrels, or by 1.7 million bpd, in October as Gulf exports recovered much faster than global oil demand.
The rebound in exports from the Persian Gulf was mostly led by crude oil volumes, the IEA noted.
The November supply and demand balances suggest that the global oil market will return to a surplus this quarter, with a more substantial build in 2027, according to the agency.
However, diesel tightness persists, and product supply in the diesel market “remains the overriding concern of the broader market and consumers,” the IEA said.

Diesel Crunch Persists Despite Signs of Easing

James Noel-Beswick, Head of Commodities at Sparta Commodities, last week said that the November builds in diesel stocks would not be enough to materially ease the tight market in the first quarter of 2027.
Sparta Commodities still sees “a strong bull case” for early next year, as its analysts “still don’t believe that diesel builds are enough for Q1; a colder winter predicted only adds to this,” Noel-Beswick added.
In the United States, diesel margins remain materially higher than gasoline margins. While gasoline margins have dropped to about $20 per barrel at around pre-war levels, diesel margins at $80 per barrel are twice as high as they were before the war despite falling from the record $118 per barrel in September, according to data compiled by Reuters columnist Ron Bousso.
In Europe, the diesel margins have fallen by a third to about $60 per barrel. Yet, this is triple the average diesel margins in 2025.
Hedge funds and other portfolio managers bet on eased diesel markets. Last week, money managers slashed their bullish bets on European gasoil and on NYMEX diesel to the lowest since January, before the war in Iran upended markets, according to futures data compiled by Bloomberg.
London gasoil, the benchmark for diesel, dipped by 9% last week to $157 per barrel, compared with about $200 at the beginning of November. U.S. diesel futures have also dropped, with the New York ULSD contract trading down around 7% last week, Ole Hansen, Head of Commodity Strategy at Saxo Bank, wrote in an analysis on Friday.
If diesel and other fuel prices remain on the downward trend and no escalation in the Middle East disrupts supply, the normalization of diesel margins and prices could gradually reverse part of the inflationary impulse, although the pass-through to consumer prices will take time, Hansen added.

Oil tanker freight rates plunge in Asia as Strait of Hormuz attacks disrupt fuel shipments

OilNOW · November 19, 2026
Oil tanker freight rates across Asia-Pacific have fallen sharply as attacks on commercial vessels near the Strait of Hormuz disrupt refined fuel shipments, leaving more tankers competing for fewer cargoes.
S&P Global reported on November 18 that Medium Range (MR) tanker freight rates dropped by 125 Worldscale points on a benchmark Middle East route, as security concerns slowed vessel movements through the critical shipping passage.
“Cargo flows are limited; there are hardly any refined products coming out from the Persian Gulf. Several tankers are looking for employment and ready to snap up cargoes at lower rates,” a senior executive at a clean oil tanker company told S&P Global.
According to UK Maritime Trade Operations, three commercial vessels were attacked in the Persian Gulf and waters off Oman over two days.
Wood Mackenzie cuts Q4 global crude run forecast by 1.4 million b/d as Middle East conflict drags on
The growing risks have prompted many shipping companies to avoid the Strait, while others wait for vessels inside the Persian Gulf to transport fuel to ship-to-ship transfer locations in Oman and western India.
Daily vessel transits through Hormuz fell to just 14 on November 9, compared with 32 at the end of October, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea data. Brokers estimated that fewer than six refined-product tankers were passing through the Strait on an average day.
The disruption is already affecting freight negotiations.
Brokers reported that Vitol provisionally booked the Torm Stellar at Worldscale 500 for November 25 diesel loading on the Duqm-East Africa route. Another tanker, Weco Amalie, was subsequently placed at Worldscale 475 for the Sikka-East Africa route, representing a decline of 125 points from the previous comparable fixture.
Iran says U.S. failing to meet conditions for reopening of Hormuz Strait
The weakness has spread to North Asia, where refined-product exports from China have fallen short of expectations despite the government announcing approximately 5.65 million metric tons of additional export quotas in late October.
On the South Korea-Japan route, the Oriental Sunstone was provisionally booked for US$975,000, marking the first reported fixture below US$1 million since late August.
Lower MR freight rates are also prompting some charterers to consider splitting larger fuel shipments into smaller parcels rather than using Long Range (LR) tankers.

Market Insight
By Nikos Tagoulis, Head of Research Department
The diesel market saw a series of notable developments last
week, against a backdrop of elevated prices and mounting con-
cerns over energy security. The G7 agreed to release 100 million
barrels of crude and diesel stocks over the next four months,
pending the IEA’s decision on the details and implementation of
the stock release. Europe is expected to contribute around 50
million barrels of diesel, further drawing down strategic invento-
ries. At the same time, commercial stocks in the ARA hub remain
below their five-year average, revealing a relatively limited buffer.
The release move followed US pressure and discussions aimed at
removing the threat of restrictions on US diesel exports.
Supply uncertainty is also mounting elsewhere. China suspended
refined-product exports around the Golden Week holiday, follow-
ing a sharp increase in diesel exports during September, leaving
uncertainty over policy thereafter. Russia, meanwhile, remains
largely sidelined from the export market following the extension
of its diesel restrictions through October and continued disruption
to refining infrastructure from Ukrainian attacks.
In the Middle East, the recovery in crude exports observed has not
been matched by refined products. Vortexa data indicate regional
diesel/gasoil exports reached 1.12 mbpd in September, down 36%
y-o-y, while flows to Europe were roughly 50% lower. Lower Mid-
dle Eastern product exports are particularly relevant for Europe,
given its dependence on the region for diesel imports.
Across the Atlantic, the US remains a critical diesel supplier. US
diesel/gasoil exports reached around 1.57 mbpd in Q3 2026, up
28% y-o-y, supported by strong flows into Central and South
America alongside increasing long-haul shipments to Europe by
approx. 35% y-o-y. While intra-American trades are relatively
short-haul, stronger US Gulf-Europe shipments add ton miles and
provide meaningful support for MR employment. Keeping US ex-
ports unrestricted also preserves a crucial source of incremental
Atlantic Basin diesel supply.
Within this constrained supply environment, Europe is increasing-
ly turning to alternative suppliers beyond the US, with India
emerging as a more prominent source. October arrivals of diesel/
gasoil from India are currently expected at around 228k bpd, up
approximately 65% m-o-m. India is well placed to respond to the
global supply deficit, supported by a large refining base fed by
crude mainly from Russia and the Middle East, while New Delhi’s
recent reduction in the diesel export levy provides further support
for increased export flows. Strong European margins could attract
more Indian barrels westward, providing further support to LR1/
LR2 employment and ton-mile demand.
Longer-haul arbitrage opportunities may also emerge from
Northeast Asia, with a 90,000-ton South Korean diesel cargo re-
portedly fixed for Northwest Europe. This trade stands out, given
Korea’s traditional focus on more proximate markets such as
Australia and East Asia. However, Korea’s ability to respond more
broadly to stronger global diesel demand remains constrained by
government energy-security measures, which cap monthly ex-
ports of regular gasoline, automotive diesel and heating kerosene
at the volumes shipped in the corresponding month of 2025.
For product tanker demand, these developments are broadly sup-
portive. Europe’s need to source barrels from the US Gulf, India
and potentially South Korea, supports ton-mile demand across
both the MR and LR segments. European strategic-stock releases
could temporarily reduce prompt import requirements, but unless
underlying supply constraints ease materially, the redirection of
diesel trade flows towards more distant suppliers should remain
supportive of tanker utilisation.
More broadly, should elevated diesel prices and constrained mar-
ket conditions persist, the impact could extend beyond the prod-
uct-tanker market. Heavy industry, road transportation and agri-
culture remain highly reliant on diesel, while short-term demand
is relatively inelastic . Persistently high costs could intensify infla-
tionary pressures and weigh on agricultural economics, affecting
production and exports and create a secondary spillover beyond
product tankers into dry bulk, impacting seaborne grain volumes.
Overall, the current diesel imbalance is increasingly reshaping
trade routes, as Europe’s search for replacement barrels supports
longer-haul product flows.

Three tankers loaded with Russian diesel have arrived in or rerouted toward Brazil after U.S. buyers and officials declined the shipments over sanctions risks, the shipping industry outlet The Maritime Executive reported Thursday.
The diversions follow controversy over an Oct. 9 Russian diesel supply deal between U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. While the vessels were headed towards the U.S., American fuel importers balked at purchasing the cargoes due to reputational risks and warnings from officials despite the Trump administration’s sanctions waiver.
According to the Maritime Executive, the Sierra Leone-flagged tanker Leruo reached the Itacoatiara anchorage in Brazil earlier this week before continuing up the Amazon River toward Manaus. The Russian-flagged Primorye also reportedly arrived at the Itacoatiara anchorage closely behind the Leruo.
The Sierra Leone-flagged Beast was said to be sailing off the South American coast with its tracking signal listed as “Brazil For Orders.” Each vessel is reportedly carrying around 40,000 metric tons of diesel.
Brazilian importers were offered at least four cargoes of a combined 1.1 million barrels of Russian diesel this month, Sérgio Araújo, president of the fuel importers’ association Abicom, told Bloomberg last week.

If Brazil were to buy all four cargoes, the volume would be nearly twice what it imported from Russia in October. Traders said at the time that prices were not as attractive as those of U.S.-made fuel.
Brazil relies on imports for about a third of its diesel needs. Demand typically peaks toward the end of the year as farmers use more fuel to run machinery and truckers haul fertilizer.
The Maritime Executive reported that other tankers initially tracked by the environmental group Greenpeace as potentially heading toward the U.S. have also changed course. The Russian-flagged Talisman was recently spotted in the Mediterranean off Egypt, while the Malta-flagged and Greek-owned Agioi Fanendes has remained idling several hundred miles out in the Atlantic for more than a week, with its status set to “For Orders.”

Japan's purchase of up to 8 million barrels is modest against global flows, but it adds a source of committed demand just as oil sells off on surplus fears . Japan is restocking its emergency reserves with Saudi crude and giving Riyadh three times more room to store oil on Japanese soil, a sign that this year's Gulf disruptions are pushing buyers and sellers toward deeper supply partnerships.
Summary:
* Japan will buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to refill its strategic petroleum reserve
* Saudi Arabia gains access to a further 16 million barrels of storage in Japan, on top of 8 million already available
* Saudi Arabia supplied 42% of Japan's crude imports in 2025, with the UAE close behind at 41%
* The Middle East accounted for 93% of Japan's total oil imports
* The deal secures supply for Japan and a reliable outlet for Saudi exports
* MUFG expects more storage deals and wider access for Gulf exporters after this year's disruptions
Japan and Saudi Arabia have agreed a strategic oil storage arrangement that will see Tokyo buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to refill its petroleum reserve, while Riyadh gains significantly more space to store oil on Japanese soil. Under the deal, Saudi Arabia will have access to a further 16 million barrels of storage capacity in Japan, adding to the 8 million barrels it already had and tripling its total to 24 million barrels, according to a note from MUFG.
The agreement reflects Japan's heavy dependence on Gulf supply. Saudi Arabia was Japan's largest source of crude imports in 2025, accounting for 42% of the total, with the United Arab Emirates close behind at 41%. Overall, oil from the Middle East made up 93% of Japan's imports, leaving the country among the most exposed of the major consumers to disruption in the region.
That exposure has been tested this year, as conflict in the Middle East disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and pushed consumer nations to draw on emergency stocks. Refilling those reserves is now a priority for importers, and long-term supply relationships offer a way to rebuild them with greater certainty.
The benefits run both ways. For Japan, a larger and more durable link with its biggest supplier helps secure access to crude in a crisis. For Saudi Arabia, storage in Japan provides a reliable destination for its exports and positions barrels close to major Asian buyers, allowing quicker deliveries when supply chains are strained elsewhere.
MUFG expects the model to spread. It sees scope for existing storage facilities to be expanded, and for Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern exporters to secure storage access in a wider range of countries, as both producers and consumers look to guard against a repeat of this year's disruption. With oil prices under pressure from expectations of a looming surplus, such arrangements could also help Gulf exporters lock in demand as their shipments recover.

Petrobras ships 950,000 barrels of pre-salt crude to Japan for first time

By EL7 News Desk
    

Key Facts

1 Petrobras exported about 950,000 barrels of crude from the Libra field to Japan for the first time, purchased by Idemitsu Kosan.
2 The Middle East accounted for 94% of Japan’s crude oil imports in 2025.
3 Brazil’s crude exports totaled 93.3 million metric tons between January and October 2026, up 16% year on year.
4 Japan’s imports of Middle Eastern crude fell 67.2% year on year in April 2026 to 3.8 million cubic meters.
Petrobras exported pre-salt oil to Japan for the first time, shipping about 950,000 barrels from the Libra field in the Santos Basin, purchased by Idemitsu Kosan, according to a report published by eixos on November 25, 2026. The MT C Creator tanker left the field carrying the crude in a deal that opens a new route into an Asian market for the Brazilian producer. The company said it is strengthening ties with overseas markets, opening new business opportunities and expanding them. The move comes as Japan relies heavily on crude imports from the Middle East. The region accounted for 94% of Japan’s oil imports in 2025, according to data from Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry cited in the report.
The cargo was transferred at Malaysia’s Kuala Sungai Linggi port to the MT Mayasan, chartered by the buyer, according to the report. The crude is due to be processed into fuel, Petrobras said. The transport route places a Malaysian port between the Brazilian production field and the Japanese destination, while the cargo remains tied to a specific Japanese buyer. The report did not state when the tanker is expected to arrive in Japan. The operation marks the first documented export of Brazilian pre-salt crude to the country, according to the company as quoted in the report.
Japan remains an uncommon market for Brazilian crude: Comex Stat recorded exports there in May 2010 and December 2021, without identifying the exporting companies. The volume was 134,000 metric tons in May 2010, then 131,000 metric tons in December 2021. These records show that trade between the two countries predates the current cargo, but was not a recurring route or previously linked to a named exporter in the system’s data. The Libra cargo stands out as the first pre-salt export to Japan and because the report named Idemitsu Kosan as its buyer. The report did not compare the size of the current cargo with those earlier shipments using a common unit of measurement.
The sale comes as Japan’s imports of Middle Eastern crude fell 67.2% year on year in April 2026 to 3.8 million cubic meters, the lowest monthly volume in the series that began in 1979. Separate data from Japan’s Ministry of Economy show that the country imported 139,735,617 kiloliters of crude in 2025, including 130,676,588 kiloliters from the Middle East. Saudi Arabia Expands Oil Storage in Japan to 24 Million Barrels

FxBrokerTrust
2026-11-25 07:56
Summary
Japan's METI and Saudi Arabia announced on 20 November that Japan will buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to replenish its strategic reserves, while offering Saudi Arabia an additional 16 million barrels of storage, tripling its capacity in Japan to about 24 million barrels. Saudi Arabia accounted for 42% of Japan's crude imports in 2025.
Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry ( METI ) and Saudi Arabia issued a joint statement on 20 November announcing an expansion of oil storage cooperation: Japan will purchase up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to replenish its national petroleum reserves, while providing Saudi Arabia with an additional 16 million barrels of storage capacity. Combined with the kingdom's existing 8 million barrels of storage, its capacity in Japan will triple to around 24 million barrels.
Japan is topping up its emergency reserves with Saudi crude and granting Riyadh three times as much storage space within its borders, signalling that this year's Gulf supply disruptions are pushing buyers and sellers towards deeper supply cooperation.

Key Points of the Agreement

* Japan will purchase up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to replenish its strategic petroleum reserves, subject to favourable market conditions and the completion of necessary domestic procedures;
* Saudi Arabia will gain an additional 16 million barrels of storage space in Japan on top of its existing 8 million barrels, bringing the total to around 24 million barrels;
* In 2025, Saudi Arabia accounted for 42% of Japan's crude imports, closely followed by the United Arab Emirates at 41%;
* The Middle East accounts for 93% of Japan's total oil imports;
* The agreement secures supply for Japan while providing a reliable outlet for Saudi exports.

Japan's Heavy Reliance on Gulf Supply

The agreement reflects Japan's heavy dependence on Gulf supply. In 2025, Saudi Arabia was Japan's largest source of crude imports, accounting for 42% of the total. Overall, oil from the Middle East made up 93% of Japan's imports, making the country one of the major consumers most exposed to supply disruptions in the region.
That vulnerability was tested this year, when conflict in the Middle East disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and forced consuming nations to draw on emergency reserves. Replenishing those stockpiles has now become a priority for importers, and long-term supply relationships offer a route to rebuilding reserves with greater certainty.
This is a mutually beneficial arrangement. For Japan, a larger and more durable link with its biggest supplier helps secure access to crude in times of crisis. For Saudi Arabia, storing oil in Japan provides a reliable destination for its exports and positions crude close to a major Asian buyer, enabling faster delivery when supply chains elsewhere come under strain.

Storage Cooperation Model May Spread

Japan's purchase of up to 8 million barrels is modest relative to global crude trade flows, but it adds a measure of certain demand at a time when the market is selling off crude amid oversupply concerns. Restocking by consuming nations that drew down emergency reserves this year could lend support to near-term crude demand.
Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group ( MUFG ) expects this model to be replicated more widely. The bank believes there is room to expand existing storage facilities, and that Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern exporters are likely to gain storage access in more countries, as both producers and consumers seek to guard against a repeat of this year's supply disruptions. Should other importers strike similar arrangements, the trend would cement Middle Eastern exporters' long-term hold over Asian demand. Such deals could also help Gulf exporters lock in demand as shipments recover, against a backdrop of oil prices pressured by expectations of oversupply.
(Source: Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, Joint Statement on Energy Security Cooperation between Japan and Saudi Arabia , published: 2026-11-20.)

TAIPEI —
Taiwan's army has put a NT$24.68 million purchase of night-vision and tethered multirotor drones back out to tender, according to a notice posted on the government's e-procurement system on 24 November. Bids close on 8 December and will be opened that afternoon in Taipei.
The notice, issued for the Army Command Headquarters by its logistics command's procurement office, keeps the case number and budget of a first tender published on 16 April. That round, with bids due on 5 May, never reached a contract: a notice dated 20 November said the army would not open or award it because the tender documents had been changed or supplemented, and that it would restart the purchase under the same case number.
Bidders must post a NT$740,000 bid bond and can download the tender papers online, but bids have to be delivered by post or by hand to the logistics command's tender room in Taipei's Nangang district rather than filed electronically, the notice says. The army set 27 November as the deadline for suppliers to raise questions about the documents.

Fixed price, no Chinese parts

The army will pick a supplier through a most-advantageous-tender process, and the winner must deliver within 180 days of the day after the contract is signed, with Tainan named as the place of delivery, the notice shows. The Liberty Times reported that the price is fixed and will not be scored.
According to the paper, the tender rules out drones made in China and parts or raw materials sourced from China, and a local company offering a foreign product must attach the import declaration. The notice does not say how many drones the army wants, nor does it give camera specifications, tether height or flight time, the Liberty Times said.

Watching for hours on a cable

A tethered drone draws power through a cable from equipment on the ground, so it is not limited by battery life the way a normal multirotor drone is, and some systems also pass video and data down the line. That suits long watches over a fixed spot, such as guarding a camp, while night-vision drones carry low-light or infrared thermal cameras to help ground units see in the dark, the Liberty Times said.
The money was set aside in the army's 2026 budget to test whether the drones are worth buying. The Liberty Times reported in August 2025 that the budget plan listed NT$24.675 million for an evaluation of night-vision and tethered drones and a further NT$6.147 million for fibre-optic drones, which are controlled through an optical fibre and so are not affected by electronic jamming.
The paper added that in November 2025 the army asked suppliers to offer 70 training drones and four tethered power modules, which had to have satellite positioning, hovering and automatic return or slow descent, and no Chinese-made parts. It said the army has not explained whether that earlier buy is linked to the new tender.

Taiwan's Navy Tenders NT$36 Billion for 280 VTOL Drones

Bids close 15 December. The notice names no aircraft, but the Navy's budget plan was reported in August as 280 Shield AI V-BATs.
Delfim de Almeida Nov 24, 2026 | 3 min read
Illustration of a generic tail-sitting drone with a ducted fan standing upright on the flight deck of a grey patrol ship, beside a rugged control case
Illustration
Spotted Nov 24, 2026 by FlightBrief's archive , which watches Taiwan's government procurement system, read by FlightBrief's tenders script.
Taiwan’s defence ministry has opened a NT$35.97 billion tender for vertical take-off drones for its navy, about US$1.1 billion. The notice went up on the government procurement system on 16 November, and bids close on 15 December.
It is the largest call on FlightBrief’s list of open drone tenders by some distance. The ministry’s procurement office runs it on behalf of Navy Command and lists the item only as “smart vertical take-off and landing drones”. It names no aircraft and no maker.

What the money buys

The numbers behind the budget sit in the defence ministry’s spending plan for 2027, sent to the Legislative Yuan on 31 August. As reported by the Liberty Times, the programme runs from 2026 to 2029 and costs NT$36.0 billion in all.
It buys 280 drones, 140 control systems and 82 transport vehicles. The navy plans 40 drones this year and 110 in 2027, with NT$13.77 billion set aside for 2027 alone. The last 130 follow in 2028 and 2029.
The plan gives the reason in plain terms. If China ’s opening strikes knock out Taiwan’s command and communications, the navy wants drones that keep watching the sea and resist GPS jamming. They go to its surface combat groups and its littoral forces.

One aircraft in the frame

The tender is open to any qualified firm. When the budget went to the legislature in August, though, United Daily News described the 280 drones as V-BATs, the tail-sitting drone made by the American company Shield AI . The Liberty Times noted that outside attention had focused on the V-BAT, and that the notice does not specify one.
Shield AI already flies in Taiwan. On 13 October it said it had delivered the coast guard’s first V-BAT with Taiwan’s AIDC, under a contract won in July.
The rules favour a maker with a track record. Bidders must prove they have already built or supplied similar equipment, with acceptance records or invoices; a contract alone does not count. Each puts up a NT$50 million bond.
The ministry will choose the most advantageous bid rather than the cheapest, and price counts for at least 20% of the score. Only one firm wins. The purchase is marked as touching national security, and it sits outside Taiwan’s commitments under the WTO’s procurement agreement, so no foreign bidder has a treaty right to compete.

Beside the coast guard’s buy

The scale shows next to the coast guard’s own drone programme. Its officials told legislators in April that it would spend about NT$2.1 billion on 451 vertical take-off drones, Taiwanese papers reported. Its tender for the 18 medium-range drones in that plan, worth NT$782.7 million, closes on 25 November.
The navy is also buying a domestic drone in the same budget. United Daily News reported NT$16.79 billion for 32 Albatross II drones from the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology, Taiwan’s state weapons laboratory.
The bids for the 280 drones will be opened at the defence ministry in Taipei at 10:00 on 15 December. Unless at least three qualified firms have bid, the ministry will not open them.

Taiwan to acquire, develop drones to strengthen defense, boost exports

November 22, 2026
2 minute read
Taiwan military personnel display a domestically developed drone in Taichung in October 2026. ANADOLU/GETTY IMAGES
FORUM Staff
Taiwan is investing in autonomous systems, including aerial and sea drones, that have been used widely in the Russia-Ukraine and Iran conflicts. Taiwan recently approved a $7.4 billion drone defense bill, and its military wants to acquire more than 1,400 coastal surveillance and reconnaissance drones, 200,000 attack drones, and 1,320 one-way attack uncrewed surface vessels (USV), the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency reported.
Taiwan officials, defense researchers and international companies highlighted the growing importance of uncrewed maritime systems, super intelligence — also known as artificial intelligence — and domestic defense manufacturing during a sea drone exhibition in Taipei in late October 2026. The event showcased how sea drones can monitor around Taiwan, a self-governed island that the Chinese Communist Party threatens to annex by force.
Taipei is prioritizing developing uncrewed systems technologies for economic and strategic reasons. It seeks to supply trusted uncrewed systems to international partners while strengthening Taiwan’s ability to defend itself.
To become a top drone exporter, Taipei must establish three pillars to a domestic industry, officials said at the Taiwan Drone International Forum: forge supply chains that do not involve China; develop and integrate super intelligence into autonomous platforms such as uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAV) to allow decision-making and navigation even during jamming attempts; and finalize international partnerships to allow joint research and development, technology transfers, and collaborative manufacturing.
Demand is spurring the effort. Taiwan exported about 210,000 drones worth $237.6 million between January and July 2026, already surpassing its 2025 total, the Taipei-based CommonWealth Magazine reported.
Taiwan has the expertise and industrial foundation to manufacture sea drones, analysts say, noting electronics manufacturers, precision-machinery suppliers, and motor producers and manufacturers can produce uncrewed systems. Taiwan also is seeking partners to produce battle-tested systems with enhanced software. For instance, the Taiwan Coast Guard plans to buy 25 USVs from United States-based Maritime Tactical Systems that will be manufactured in Taiwan and the U.S.
“If you’ve got a lot of small USVs out there doing a lot of different missions, it really takes a load off of the Coast Guard and the Navy and what some of their gray hull ships are doing,” company executive Seamus Flatley told AFP.
Sea drones, which can be built faster than a warship or submarine, are a relatively low-cost asset that can complicate an adversary’s plans. Global interest in uncrewed underwater vehicles also has soared since the Middle East conflict began in February 2026.
“We have seen a significant increase in demand as people start to realize that you can just have a very simple mine destroy a whole entire [maritime] channel, and that’s where underwater robots come in to neutralize these targets,” Grace Chia, chief executive of BeeX, an autonomous underwater vehicle manufacturer in Singapore, told AFP.

Taiwan's drone exports rose 34-fold to 122,726 units in 2025, but the industry behind them lacks certification, supply-chain depth and an order from its own military, which holds fewer than 5,000 drones.
Surveyed November 22, 2026
Reading 8 min read
Correspondent Sophie Lindqvist
Taiwan’s drone industry looks like it's booming. Inside, the picture is much shakier. Taiwan’s drone industry looks like it's booming. Inside, the picture is much shakier. — Lucent_Designs_dinoson20 / pixabay

Field notes

1. Drone exports jumped 34-fold, from 3,500 units in 2024 to 122,726 in 2025, reaching 191,373 units by June 2026
2. Overseas drone sales rose from $4.2 million in 2024 to $89 million in 2025 and $277 million in the first eight months of 2026

...

"We hope that even if we don't have the war demand, maybe there will be civilian or government use to sustain it," she said.
Dennis Huang, managing director for international strategy and operations at drone maker Taiwan UAV, is blunter about the source of the edge. "The Taiwan drone industry exists or is able to be competitive because of the split from non-Chinese drone components," he said. "If that didn't exist or no one cared about it, I don't think the Taiwan drone industry will be competitive at all."
The series also lacks stability. Exports spiked to roughly 136,000 drones in the first quarter of 2026, then fell to 55,300 in the second, and monthly data through September peak in March at 54,978 units. Cumulative exports had reached 191,373 units by June 2026.

Who is actually building them?

...

Bryce Barros, a visiting researcher at the government-funded Institute for National Defense and Security Research (INDSR), credits Taiwan's many small and medium-sized firms with the ability to pivot quickly into new work. In July, Hocheng Corp, a maker of toilet ceramics, said publicly it is producing external armour for vehicles and moving into drone composites.

Does the China-free label survive procurement?

Phoebe Pham, an INDSR researcher and former RAND analyst, says Taiwan has no centralised route for manufacturers to learn military requirements and reach government buyers. She points to Ukraine's Brave1 and DOT-Chain marketplaces, where makers list products, meet one another and read what troops need.

...

Jiin Ming said it was cooperating with authorities and had "consistently maintained our commitment to a non-China supply chain."
Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs said lawmakers are establishing a drone committee to strengthen "interagency policy coordination and resource integration," and that certification standards for verifying the origin of drone parts will be developed "as soon as possible."

Why isn't Taiwan's own military ordering?

Fewer than 5,000 drones sit in the military's arsenal, according to Fang's August assessment. The government sought $6.6 billion last year to buy roughly 210,000 drones by 2031, and opposition lawmakers blocked that funding for eight months. A revised $7.6 billion plan still requires annual spending approvals, and the money may not flow until 2027.
Large domestic orders would give suppliers the confidence to hire and invest, Fang said, while the delay costs time needed for testing, data collection and training AI models in a market that changes monthly. Huang said the funding dispute stalled major tenders Taiwan UAV intended to bid for, including one for loitering munitions, the drones that circle a target before striking.
The presidential office said it is seeking $1.7 billion this year for naval and aerial drones and is looking to civilian and international buyers to sustain the sector. Meanwhile the US is moving faster through its Drone Dominance programme, which identifies approved systems through the Blue UAS list.

How long does the China-free window last?

...

For a foreign buyer, this is still a war-supply market: cheap systems, volatile quarterly volumes, and Polish and Czech orders that may evaporate with a ceasefire. For an investor, the China-free premium carries a two-to-five-year half-life unless Taiwan climbs the value chain, and the certification regime due "as soon as possible" is the gating item. Watch three developments: the certification rules, annual budget approvals before 2027, and whether the $1.7 billion request reaches a purchase order.
A sector can post a 34-fold export gain and still fail to supply the one customer that would make it durable. Taiwan's own military is that customer.

This briefing outlines the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' (USACE) plan to utilize Other Transactional Authority (OTA) with Construction Manager at Risk (CM@R) delivery for upcoming Marine Corps Energy Resilience Readiness Program (ERCIP) projects in Japan. OTAs operate outside the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) under 10 U.S.C. § 2808a, offering flexibility, commercial best practices, and collaborative arrangements, while remaining subject to fiscal law, cybersecurity, and environmental regulations. The CM@R process engages the construction contractor early during design to enhance constructability, cost control, and scheduling. Procurement involves a two-step solicitation: a Request for Qualifications/White Papers, followed by interactive pitch presentations with top-ranked firms. Awards occur in two phases: Phase 1 covers negotiated preconstruction services, and Phase 2 establishes a Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP) for construction. If a GMP agreement is not reached, the government may competitively solicit construction elsewhere. The pipeline comprises five resilient microgrid projects in Japan: 1. Camp Fuji (FY25 P904): Target award May 2028. 2. MCAS Iwakuni (FY26 P1016): Target award Feb 2029. 3. Camp Foster (FY30 P312): Target award Feb 2029. 4. Camp Hansen (FYTBD P-625): Award TBD. 5. Camp Courtney (FYTBD P406): Award TBD. Each project involves constructing resilient energy systems integrating natural gas/diesel generators, solar photovoltaic systems, battery energy storage systems (BESS), utility interconnections, controls, commissioning, and cybersecurity to ensure uninterrupted power for warfighters.
